toc.title: What this does, and doesn't do

blocks.p: You've probably learned about the Polyvagal Theory, how your nervous system shifts between safety, flight, fight, and shutdown. And now you're asking yourself, okay, now what? The first tip was identifying your polyvagal state. This second tip is about increasing passive safety cues through your environment.

By the end, you'll better understand safety cues in general and passive safety cues in particular. You'll also have at least one very specific, very practical thing you can do now to access your safety state a bit more than yesterday, and you'll be set up to do the same thing tomorrow.

As mammals, in the most basic sense, our autonomic nervous systems can exist in a state of safety and connection, sympathetic flight and fight, or collapsed shutdown. That's very basic Polyvagal Theory. Easy peasy.

So obviously we want more safety activation, right? Of course. How do we get it? We need to cue safety. Our brain needs to realize that it's safe, and not on a cognitive level. I'm talking about a much deeper, very basic, organismic level. Even though you may consciously know that you're safe, that doesn't mean the rest of your body does.

When you're anxious, I could ask you, "Are you literally safe?" And you'd say something like, "Yeah, no poop, Justin. Why are you bothering me?" And then of course my feelings would be hurt. The point is that your thinking, conscious brain knows it's safe in a very literal sense, but it's like the rest of your body doesn't believe it.
Why is this? Because the brainstem needs to receive safety cues.

The brainstem is really the most important aspect of the Polyvagal Theory, not the vagus nerve. The brainstem is where all of the state shifting takes place. Your body and the rest of your brain communicate with the brainstem. It's the middle point. It receives signals from both the body and the brain, and then uses those signals to shift your state to whatever is necessary in that moment. Dr. Porges put it this way when he was on the podcast: "What higher brain structures can do are in part limited by the state that the brainstem is in." ([Episode 15](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/a3c6a54a-11a7-4f2f-9d74-db287c774d08))
The brainstem is also the thing that continually tells your autonomic nervous system that it's in danger, keeping you stuck in a defensive, traumatized state.

So the way to optimally use your polyvagal knowledge is not to try stimulating your vagus nerve, or gargling, or humming, or whatever hack you're trying. Instead, it's as simple as increasing the cues of safety your brainstem is receiving. Give it more cues of safety and it will take care of the rest. It will shift your autonomic state toward safety and away from defense.

Does this release your stuck trauma? No, not by itself. But continually feeding your brainstem cues of safety will help increase its access to safety, and give you the platform you need to work on your trauma and relieve your stuck defensive state, if that's your goal.
Your brainstem can receive signals of safety from a few sources:

ol: The rest of the brain. Thinking can influence your brainstem, like remembering safety, or learning new, judgment-free information like the Polyvagal Theory. We'll call this top down.
The rest of the body. Everything happening below the brainstem. We'll call this bottom up. Singing and dancing are really great examples of cueing safety in the body.
The outside world. The things happening outside of your body can send signals of safety too. We'll call this outside in.

blocks.p: Outside in is what we'll focus on here, and more specifically, passive safety cues. These are things from the outside that you don't really have to do anything with. They just cue safety in your system passively.

The outside world can send your brainstem cues of safety or cues of defense. We want to increase the cues of safety. Deb Dana said it simply when she was on the podcast: "There have to be more cues of safety than danger in order for me to move into ventral." ([Episode 29](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c))

The problem is that we don't have much control over the outside world. We can't turn off the annoying music at the grocery store. We can't make people give us more space in line, and we can't stop the incessant loudspeaker announcing codes. We can't control the weather. And we probably don't live in a forest, or near a picturesque beach we can reach by stepping out the back door. I know I don't. If you do, good for you.

But we do have homes, and we have a lot of control over the things in our homes. If you're renting a room, you have control over your room. You can control how loud or quiet things are, and you can control the space and the lighting too. There are some restrictions, of course, but there's a lot of control we do have.

So can you bring the beach or the forest into your home? Not really. But you can turn on the sound of waves, or get a candle that smells like your favorite forest tree. You may not be able to make the perfect, magazine-ready home environment. We don't need that. You can adjust some things in your home to cue more safety now than yesterday.

Before you implement anything, focus on one area of your home. Not the entire home, not even the entire room. Maybe just a corner. One area. In my second book, [Stuck Not Broken, Book Two: Building Safety](piece:anchor-environment), I call this the passive safety environment. Pick one area to increase passive safety cues, and branch out from there as you're ready.
Here are three really easy ways to increase safety from the outside in.

You can easily increase passive safety cues through the smells of your passive safety environment. This probably won't cost you a thing, since I'm willing to bet you already have a candle or some form of aromatherapy, like a diffuser.
I just got a candle in Hawaii because it has a coconut scent, and it is awesome. Is it worth thirty bucks? Not really, but I got it anyway. I love the scent and the taste of coconut.

I also highly recommend opening the windows for a bit and letting your space air out. I find it really useful, kind of like a blank slate. Plus, if the weather's right and you can open things up, now you have a soft breeze coming in and some sunlight, providing even more layers of passive safety.

So find a scent that speaks to your system now, get it going, and that's about it. That scent will continually provide you with cues of safety, passively. Once it's on, you don't really have to think about it anymore.
This one might be a tad more challenging, and might cost something. But let's start as free as possible. You probably have curtains or some other window covering.

If you're in a dysregulated shutdown state, it might feel good to keep your curtains closed and block the light. I know it kind of feels better, but that's not the same as safety cueing. Maybe your system is ready for a bit more light. Opening your curtains a crack might be a good idea. As you get more safety in your system, opening them more and more will get easier and easier. If you need darkness at first, fine. But listen to your system. It might be ready for a little bit of light.

If you lean toward darker environments, you could also turn on a lamp in the room, a smaller spot of light, not the huge overhead lighting. If your lamp is too bright, can you dim it, add a shade, or cover it with something heat and fire resistant? Please don't start any fires.

When cueing safety through lighting, natural light is typically better than artificial for passive safety, and it's free, which is good. As much as I love natural light, I also love my smart bulbs. They might be a great idea if you have the money. I have them all around my house, even on the outside deck. I can adjust the brightness to just the right amount, and even the color they emit, and set them to come on at certain times of day. So as the sun sets, the bulbs come on all around the home to help my family and me feel super cozy. Not bright lighting, just dim lighting all around the house. It's really nice.
The last tip is physical space: making sure you have enough room to sit, lie down, stand up, do yoga, or whatever else you want.

There's no right amount of space. You'll need to listen to your body. I'm sure you know what too little space is like, sitting next to strangers in a stadium. But for you, what's the right amount of space, the amount that helps you feel more comfortable and breathe easier?

I'm a fairly tall drink of water at six feet, and I bump into things far too often. I need a lot of space. I do not do well in cramped environments. So when I set up my passive safety environments in my home office and in my therapy office, I made sure to include enough space to feel good for me.

Physical space also includes the tidiness of your passive safety environment. Is your desk clear, or do you have a bunch of cords and crumbs and an old cup of coffee lying around? Can you actually sit on your chair or your couch, or is your kids' or your spouse's stuff there? Or maybe it's your own stuff that you threw down after work. I know you're going to get to it, but it is there. Maybe it's time to get rid of stuff, to declutter, to tidy, to clean up.

blocks.h: What this does, and doesn't do

blocks.p: Again, this doesn't release your trauma. It doesn't solve all your mental health problems. What it does is lay a nice, solid foundation: a place you can go to breathe a bit easier, maybe even smile, a place to relax and calm down. And from that foundation, you could go further and start to feel other things you have inside of you. That really is how you get unstuck.

Now you know about passive safety cues, and about the brainstem, instead of trying to hack your vagus nerve. Hopefully you're ready to simplify and focus on one area of your home to start creating a passive safety environment.
You don't need to create the perfect environment. You don't even need to get halfway there. Make one adjustment to your space. Pick one thing to change. Some easy options:

ul: Is there a candle or other good-smelling source you can put on?
Is there clutter you can declutter?
Is there a curtain to open?
Are there cords you can hide?
Are there crumbs to vacuum up?
Is there a dusty lamp that's ready to give you some warm lighting again?

blocks.p: Just pick one and make it happen now. We want small, sustainable steps, not large overhauls that will overwhelm you. I'm not asking you to paint this room or move the furniture around. Just one thing. Tomorrow, you can take it a step further if you like.
